title: Fewest Deletions to Match Two Words
statement:
You get two words, a and b. In one step you delete a single character from either word. Characters you keep stay in their original order.

Return the fewest steps needed to make the two words identical. Deleting everything is always allowed, so an answer always exists.

examples.why: Delete the r from each word and both become "bake". The r is in both words, but in different places, so it cannot be kept.
No characters in common: both words must be deleted completely.
Keep "bab": delete the first a of "abab" and the last a of "baba". Matching letters greedily from the front would keep less.

constraints: a and b contain lowercase English letters
hints: Whatever survives in both words is a common subsequence. Which common subsequence should you keep?
The longest one. If it has length L, the answer is a.length + b.length − 2·L.
Fill a table over prefixes: if a[i−1] equals b[j−1], extend the diagonal by 1; otherwise take the better of dropping one character from either word.

explain.intuition:
After the deletions, both words become the same string, and that string is a subsequence of each. Every character you delete is one not in that kept string. So minimizing deletions means keeping the longest common subsequence: answer = |a| + |b| − 2·LCS.

LCS is a classic table over prefixes. dp[i][j] is the LCS of the first i characters of a and the first j of b. If the last characters match, they can both be kept: dp[i−1][j−1] + 1. If not, one of them is not in the answer, so take max(dp[i−1][j], dp[i][j−1]). Text diff tools use the same table to show which lines were kept.
steps: Make a table of size (n + 1) × (m + 1) filled with 0.
For i from 1 to n and j from 1 to m: if a[i−1] === b[j−1], set dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j−1] + 1.
pitfalls: Greedily matching equal letters from the front. In "abab" vs "baba" pairing the first a's keeps only 2 letters instead of 3.
Counting shared letters regardless of order (a multiset intersection). "abcde" and "edcba" share every letter but keep only one.
Subtracting LCS once instead of twice: the kept string survives in both words.

solutions.title: Longest common subsequence table
solutions.idea: Compute the LCS over all prefix pairs; everything outside it gets deleted from both words.

solutions.title: Count deletions directly, one row
solutions.idea: Let the table hold the deletions themselves: matching last letters cost nothing extra; otherwise delete one of them for 1 more step. Keep only the previous row.

followups: Each deletion now costs the character's code point. Which line of the table changes?
Also allow replacing a character in one step. What is this problem called?
